When you call something "old hat," you mean it is outdated, no longer new, or so familiar that it has lost its freshness and excitement. It describes something that used to be new or impressive but is now considered ordinary, behind the times, or stale.

Think of it this way: imagine someone showing you a flip phone in 2026 and acting like it's the latest technology. You might say, "That's old hat!" — meaning, that idea or thing is long past its time.

This idiom carries two shades of meaning that are connected to each other. It helps to understand both.

Meaning 1 — Outdated / Old-fashioned:
Something is no longer modern or relevant. It belongs to the past.

"Using a fax machine in a modern office is old hat."

Here, the focus is on the thing itself being behind the times.

Meaning 2 — Overly familiar / Nothing new:
Something is so well-known or so commonly done that it holds no surprise or novelty anymore. It is routine.

"Don't worry about explaining the process to her — it's old hat to her. She's been doing it for 20 years."

Here, the focus is on the person's familiarity with the thing. She knows it so deeply that it feels completely ordinary.

Both meanings share the same root idea: the spark of newness is completely gone.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The origin of "old hat" goes back to 18th-century England, and the most widely accepted explanation connects it to hat fashion.

Hats were once a very important part of everyday dress. People's hat styles were closely watched as a signal of how up-to-date and stylish they were. Hat fashions changed frequently — just like clothing fashions do today. So, wearing an old hat — one that had fallen out of fashion — was a visible sign that you were behind the times. You weren't keeping up with the world around you.

Over time, this idea of the outdated hat became a general metaphor. People began using "old hat" to describe any idea, thing, or method that had grown stale or obsolete — not just actual hats.

The phrase appeared in English writing as far back as the early 1700s and has been in steady use ever since.

This idiom carries a mildly dismissive or unimpressed tone. When you use it, you are signalling that something fails to impress you because it is not new. However, it is not a harsh or rude expression — it is more casual and gently critical.

It can sometimes carry a tone of boredom — like you have seen or heard something so many times that you cannot get excited about it anymore.

Depending on context, it can also sound slightly condescending — as if you are telling someone that what they are presenting is already well-known and not worth making a fuss over.

Here are several examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits into conversation and writing.

In technology:

"Paper maps are old hat now that everyone has GPS on their phone."

In business:

"That marketing strategy might have worked in the 90s, but it's old hat today."

When talking about someone's skill:

"Public speaking used to scare him, but after hundreds of presentations, it's old hat."

In conversation:

"They kept telling us about their new product, but honestly, the concept was old hat — other companies had done the same thing years ago."

In a dismissive comment:

"Oh, that plot twist? Old hat. Every thriller from the last decade has used it."

It is important to separate "old hat" from similar-sounding ideas so you don't confuse them.

It does not mean something is bad simply because it is old. A classic novel, a well-loved tradition, or a timeless skill is not "old hat" just because it has been around for a long time. The idiom carries the sense of something being tired, stale, or no longer impressive — not merely old. For example, you would not call Shakespeare "old hat" just because he lived 400 years ago. His work is still admired and studied. But you might call a specific writing trick "old hat" if every beginner writer uses it and it no longer impresses anyone.

It is also not the same as saying something is wrong or broken. A flip phone still works perfectly. But calling it old hat means it is simply outdated compared to what is available now.

"Old hat" is an informal, conversational expression. You will find it in:

  • Everyday spoken English
  • Casual writing (blogs, opinion pieces, journalism)
  • Fiction and storytelling

You would generally avoid it in very formal writing such as legal documents, academic papers, or official business reports. In those settings, you would simply say something is "outdated," "obsolete," or "no longer relevant."

Understanding related phrases helps you see the full picture of how English speakers talk about things that are outdated or overly familiar.

"Behind the times" — Very similar. Means something or someone is not keeping up with modern developments.

"Their approach to customer service is really behind the times."

"Passé" — (borrowed from French) Means no longer fashionable or current. Slightly more formal and sometimes more sarcastic.

"Wearing fur coats is considered passé these days."

"Dated" — Means something clearly belongs to an older era and feels out of place now.

"The movie's special effects look very dated compared to today's standards."

"Been there, done that" — Used when you have already experienced something and find it unremarkable or unexciting.

"Skydiving? Been there, done that."

"Yesterday's news" — Means something is no longer interesting because everyone already knows about it or has moved on.

"That scandal is yesterday's news."

The key difference between all of these and "old hat" is a matter of emphasis and flavour. "Old hat" has a slightly more casual, breezy quality. It often implies something was once impressive but has now become too familiar to generate any excitement.

If you want to remember this idiom easily, picture this:

Imagine a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat. The first time you see it, it's magical and exciting. But after watching the same trick hundreds of times, the hat — and the trick — feel completely ordinary. That hat is now old hat. The wonder is gone. It's nothing new.

"Old hat" = something that is outdated, overly familiar, or no longer exciting because its novelty has worn off. It comes from the idea of wearing a hat that is no longer fashionable. It is a casual, mildly dismissive expression used to say that something has lost its freshness — whether because the world has moved past it, or because a person knows it so thoroughly that it feels completely routine.
